title: Fixes
sub: A problem-to-fix index for the errors you will actually hit on a Mac
goals: Match an error message to its cause in under a minute
Apply the fix as copyable commands without making things worse
Prevent the common errors in your setup instead of repeating the fix

blocks.text: Every entry has the same shape: the symptom exactly as the terminal prints it, the cause (what is really going on), and the fix as commands you can copy. Search the page for a fragment of your message. The sections run from shell basics to Python, networking and SSH, ending with a short list of general recovery moves. Breaking things is how this book teaches, so treat each entry as a drill: when the error happens, read the message first, because the message usually names the file, the command or the option at fault.

items.text: Read the last line of the error, then the first. 2. Identify the program that printed it (`zsh:`, `brew:`, `pip`, `ssh:`). 3. Reproduce with the smallest command. 4. Check one thing at a time: `type`, `which`, `echo $PATH`, `ls -l`, `file`. See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshoot) for the network version of this loop.

blocks.text: Shell errors
command not found
Symptom:

blocks.code: zsh: command not found: brew

blocks.text: Cause: zsh searched every directory in `PATH` and found no executable of that name. Either the program is not installed, the name is misspelled, or its folder is not in `PATH`. On Apple Silicon, Homebrew lives in `/opt/homebrew/bin`, which is not in the default `PATH` until your `~/.zprofile` runs `brew shellenv`.

blocks.code:
$ echo $PATH
/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin
$ ls /opt/homebrew/bin/brew
/opt/homebrew/bin/brew

blocks.text: If `ls` finds the file but `brew` does not run, fix `PATH` permanently:

blocks.code:
echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.zprofile
eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
type brew

blocks.text: For any other name, ask the shell what it knows:

blocks.code:
type {{cmd}}            # builtin, alias, function or file path
which -a {{cmd}}        # every match in PATH
echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n'
rehash                  # make zsh forget its cached command locations

blocks.text: After you install something that changes `PATH`, tabs that were already open keep the old value. Open a new tab with `⌘T`, or run `exec zsh` to restart the shell in place.
For a script in the current folder, `PATH` deliberately excludes `.`. Run it with a path:

blocks.code: ./myscript.zsh

blocks.text: zsh: command not found: python
Symptom:

blocks.code: zsh: command not found: python

blocks.text: Cause: macOS and Homebrew provide `python3`, not `python`. Inside an activated venv, `python` exists.

blocks.code:
python3 --version
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
python --version     # now defined, points into .venv

blocks.text: permission denied
Symptom (running a script):

blocks.code: zsh: permission denied: ./backup.zsh

blocks.text: Cause: the file has no execute bit. Check the mode and add it.

blocks.code:
ls -l backup.zsh            # no x in the mode string means not executable
chmod u+x backup.zsh
./backup.zsh

blocks.text: Symptom (a folder, not a file):

blocks.code: zsh: permission denied: /Users/you/projects

blocks.text: Typing a path alone tries to execute it. You wanted `cd`.
Symptom (reading or writing):

blocks.code: cat: /etc/sudoers: Permission denied

blocks.text: Cause: the file belongs to root. Use `ls -l`, then decide: `sudo` for system files you really need to read, `chown`/`chmod` for files that should be yours.

blocks.code:
ls -l /etc/sudoers
id
sudo -k                     # forget the cached password when you are done

blocks.title: Do not fix permission errors with chmod 777

blocks.text: `777` gives every user on the machine write access and removes the information the error was giving you. Find the owner (`ls -l`), then grant the minimum: `u+x` for a script, `600` for a secret, `755` for a shared folder.
Operation not permitted
Symptom:

blocks.code:
ls: .: Operation not permitted
cp: /Users/you/Library/Mail/foo: Operation not permitted

blocks.text: Cause: not Unix permissions. macOS Transparency, Consent and Control (TCC) and System Integrity Protection (SIP) protect Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Mail, Safari data and system folders. `sudo` does not override them.

Fix: System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access (or Files and Folders), add Terminal (or iTerm, PyCharm), then quit and reopen the app. SIP-protected paths such as `/System` and `/usr/bin` stay read-only on purpose; install your own tools under `/opt/homebrew` or `~/bin`.

blocks.code:
csrutil status              # reports whether SIP is enabled
ls -lO /usr/bin | head -3   # -O shows flags such as restricted

blocks.text: zsh: no matches found
Symptom:

blocks.code:
zsh: no matches found: *.txt
zsh: no matches found: requests[security]

blocks.text: Cause: zsh expands globs before the command runs. When a pattern matches no file, zsh stops with an error, where bash would pass the literal text through. Square brackets, `?` and `*` all count as globs.

blocks.code: ls *.nothing

pip install 'requests[socks]'         # quote it
find . -name '*.txt'                  # let find do the matching
ls *.txt(N)                           # N qualifier: empty list instead of an error

blocks.text: Do not disable the check globally with `setopt NO_NOMATCH` just to silence one command; the error stops `rm *.bak` from running against a pattern that matched nothing. Quote the pattern when you mean the characters.
zsh: command not found: #
Symptom (after pasting a snippet that contains comments):

blocks.code: zsh: command not found: #

blocks.text: Cause: interactive zsh does not treat `#` as a comment start by default. Scripts do; your prompt does not.

blocks.code:
setopt INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS
echo 'setopt INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS' >> ~/.zshrc

blocks.text: zsh: parse error and quoting disasters
Symptoms:

blocks.code:
zsh: parse error near `)'
dquote>
quote>
zsh: event not found: foo

blocks.text: Cause: an unbalanced or mis-nested quote. The `dquote>` and `quote>` prompts mean zsh is still waiting for the closing `"` or `'`. `event not found` means `!` triggered history expansion (`echo hi!foo` looks up a command starting with `foo`).
Fix: press [[Ctrl+C]] to abandon the line, then retype it.

head: Situation
Use
rows: Value contains `$` or backticks, you want them literal
Curly quotes pasted from a web page

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ echo 'one $HOME is not expanded'
one $HOME is not expanded
$ echo "but $HOME is"
but /Users/learner is
$ echo "a \"quoted\" word"
a "quoted" word

blocks.text: Notes apps and web pages replace `"` with typographic quotes. zsh does not see them as quote characters, so the whole word reaches the command with the odd characters attached. If a pasted command misbehaves for no visible reason, paste it into a plain text editor and compare the quotes.
Stuck commands
Symptom: nothing prints and the prompt does not return, or the screen froze.

head: Try, in order
Effect
rows: resumes output if [[Ctrl+S]] froze the terminal
end of input, for a program waiting on stdin

blocks.text: Find the process id with `pgrep -fl {{proc}}` or `ps aux | grep -i {{proc}}`. Escaping `vim`: `:q!` then [[Enter]]. Escaping `less`, `man`: `q`. Escaping `nano`: [[Ctrl+X]].
Line endings and file problems
Symptoms:

blocks.code:
zsh: ./script.sh: bad interpreter: /bin/bash^M: no such file or directory
$'\r': command not found

blocks.text: Cause: the file has Windows line endings (CRLF, `\r\n`). The invisible carriage return sticks to the end of the shebang line and to every command, so the interpreter is named `bash\r`. Check with `file`, convert with `tr` or `sed`.

blocks.code:
file script.sh                  # "... with CRLF line terminators"
tr -d '\r' < script.sh > fixed.sh && mv fixed.sh script.sh
# or, in place (the '' after -i is required on macOS):
sed -i '' $'s/\r$//' script.sh
cat -e script.sh | head -3      # lines should end in $, not ^M$ (BSD cat has no -A)

blocks.text: The reverse problem, one very long line, is a file with old Mac CR-only endings: `tr '\r' '\n' < in > out`.

Prevent it with git: `git config --global core.autocrlf input` converts CRLF to LF on commit and leaves your files alone otherwise. In PyCharm, the line separator is in the status bar at the bottom right; click it to choose `LF (\n)`.

blocks.title: Break and fix a CRLF script

task.text: Create a script with a Windows line ending on purpose, watch it fail, then repair it.

items.text: Fix it with `tr` and run it again.

hints: The shebang line is read by the kernel, which sees `/bin/bash` followed by a carriage return.
blocks.solution:
printf '#!/bin/bash\r\necho hello\r\n' > crlf.sh && chmod +x crlf.sh
./crlf.sh
file crlf.sh
tr -d '\r' < crlf.sh > ok.sh && mv ok.sh crlf.sh && chmod +x crlf.sh
./crlf.sh

why.text: The first run fails because the interpreter path ends in an invisible `\r`. `tr -d '\r'` deletes every carriage return. The `chmod` is repeated because the replacement file is new and has the default mode.

blocks.text: Homebrew and Xcode
Xcode command line tools
Symptoms:

blocks.code:
xcode-select: note: no developer tools were found at '/Applications/Xcode.app', requesting install. Choose an option in the dialog to download the command line developer tools.
xcrun: error: invalid active developer path (/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools), missing xcrun at: /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/usr/bin/xcrun

blocks.text: Cause: `git`, `make`, `clang` and Homebrew's builds rely on the Command Line Tools (CLT). A macOS update often invalidates them, producing the second error. The first line means they were never installed and a dialog has opened.

blocks.code:
xcode-select -p                 # prints the active developer directory
xcode-select --install          # opens the installer dialog; click Install and wait
softwareupdate -l               # also lists "Command Line Tools for Xcode" updates

blocks.text: If the dialog says the software is unavailable or the install keeps failing, remove the stale copy and install again:

blocks.code:
sudo rm -rf /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools
xcode-select --install

blocks.text: The `rm -rf` above targets one folder that the installer recreates. Check the path character by character before pressing [[Enter]].
brew command problems

head: Symptom
Cause
Fix
rows: `Error: The following directories are not writable by your user:`
folders under `/opt/homebrew` owned by root, often after a `sudo brew`
`sudo chown -R $(whoami) /opt/homebrew` then `chmod u+w /opt/homebrew`; never run `brew` with `sudo`
`Error: Cannot install under Rosetta 2 in ARM default prefix (/opt/homebrew)!`
the terminal is running as x86_64
a keg-only formula or missing shellenv
add the printed `export PATH=...` line to `~/.zprofile`

blocks.text: First diagnostic for anything odd:

blocks.code:
brew doctor              # read each Warning: it names the file and the remedy
brew update && brew upgrade
brew --prefix            # /opt/homebrew on Apple Silicon
brew list --versions {{pkg}}

blocks.text: `brew doctor` warns about many harmless things. Fix warnings that mention `PATH`, permissions or conflicting installs; ignore cosmetic ones.
Gatekeeper and quarantine
Symptom: "`name` cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified" or "is damaged and can't be opened" for something you downloaded and trust.
Cause: downloads carry the `com.apple.quarantine` extended attribute, which makes Gatekeeper check them on first run.

blocks.code:
xattr {{path}}                               # list attributes
xattr -d com.apple.quarantine {{path}}       # remove it for one file
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine {{path}}      # for a whole app bundle

blocks.text: On recent macOS the alternative is System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway after the first blocked attempt. Remove quarantine only from software whose source you trust.
Rosetta and architecture
Symptom: `bad CPU type in executable`, or `Cannot install under Rosetta 2 in ARM default prefix`, or tools from `/usr/local` and `/opt/homebrew` mixed up.

blocks.code:
uname -m                 # arm64 (Apple Silicon native) or x86_64 (under Rosetta)
arch                     # same information
arch -arm64 zsh          # start a native shell
arch -x86_64 zsh         # start an Intel shell, if you need one
softwareupdate --install-rosetta --agree-to-license    # Intel binaries

blocks.text: Right-click the Terminal app > Get Info and clear "Open using Rosetta" if it was ticked.
Python problems
externally-managed-environment (PEP 668)
Symptom:

blocks.code:
error: externally-managed-environment

× This environment is externally managed
╰─> To install Python packages system-wide, try brew install
    xyz, where xyz is the package you are trying to
    install.

    If you wish to install a Python library that isn't in Homebrew,
    use a virtual environment:

    python3 -m venv path/to/venv
    source path/to/venv/bin/activate
    python3 -m pip install xyz

blocks.text: Cause: the Python from Homebrew (and recent Linux distributions) marks itself as managed by its package manager, so `pip` refuses to modify its global site-packages. Mixing the two would break Homebrew's own Python tools.
Fix: one venv per project.

blocks.code:
cd ~/lab/myproject
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install {{pkg}}

blocks.text: For a command-line application you want everywhere, use `brew install {{pkg}}` if a formula exists, or `brew install pipx && pipx install {{pkg}}`. The flag `--break-system-packages` exists; it is how you break your Python installation, so do not use it.
venv will not activate, or does nothing
Symptoms:

blocks.code: zsh: no such file or directory: .venv/bin/activate

blocks.text: or the prompt shows `(.venv)` but `pip` installs go to the wrong place.

head: Check
Command
Meaning
rows: Are you in the right folder
running `./activate` does nothing: it must change your current shell
shows the site-packages it will write to
venvs contain absolute paths, copying them breaks them

blocks.code:
deactivate 2>/dev/null
rm -rf .venv
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

blocks.text: Always call `python -m pip`, not bare `pip`: it guarantees the pip belongs to the interpreter you named.
ModuleNotFoundError
Symptom:

blocks.code: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'

blocks.text: Cause: the interpreter running the script is not the one that has the package. Typical reasons: venv not active, PyCharm using a different interpreter, or installing with one Python and running another.

blocks.code:
which python3
python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable); print(sys.prefix)"
python3 -m pip list | grep -i requests
python3 -m pip install requests        # inside the active venv

blocks.text: A file named like the module also causes odd import errors: a script called `requests.py` or `random.py` shadows the real one. Rename it and delete the `__pycache__` folder.
PyCharm interpreter problems
Symptoms: a banner reading `No Python interpreter configured for the project`, red underlines on imports that work in Terminal, or `ModuleNotFoundError` only when running from PyCharm.
Cause: PyCharm keeps its own interpreter setting per project; it does not inherit whatever your shell has activated.
Fix:

items.text: Choose the interpreter list, or Add Interpreter > Add Local Interpreter > Virtualenv Environment > Existing, and select `<project>/.venv/bin/python`.
In the package list on the same page, check the missing package is present; install with the `+` button or in the terminal.
Open Settings > Tools > Terminal and tick "Activate virtualenv" so the built-in Terminal tab activates it too. Start a new Terminal tab after changing it.
Check the Run configuration (top right, Edit Configurations) uses the project interpreter.

blocks.text: Confirm from inside any script what PyCharm actually runs:

blocks.code:
import sys
print(sys.executable)

blocks.text: SSL certificate errors in Python
Symptom:

blocks.code: ssl.SSLCertVerificationError: [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: unable to get local issuer certificate

blocks.text: Cause: the python.org installer ships Python without trusted root certificates until you run its helper. Homebrew Python and PyCharm-created venvs normally work.

blocks.code:
open "/Applications/Python 3.15"       # use the folder matching your version
# double-click "Install Certificates.command", or from Terminal:
"/Applications/Python 3.15/Install Certificates.command"
python3 -m pip install --upgrade certifi
python3 -c "import certifi; print(certifi.where())"

blocks.text: If only a corporate network fails, a proxy is re-signing traffic; point `SSL_CERT_FILE` at the bundle your IT team provides. Do not disable verification (`verify=False`) except for a one-off test of your own server.
Network problems
DNS and Wi-Fi
Symptoms:

blocks.code:
ping: cannot resolve example.com: Unknown host
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: example.com
ssh: Could not resolve hostname server: nodename nor servname provided, or not known

blocks.text: Cause: the name did not turn into an address. Separate "no network" from "no DNS" by pinging an address.

blocks.code:
ping -c 2 1.1.1.1              # works? then the link is fine and DNS is the problem
ping -c 2 example.com          # fails? the resolver is the culprit
scutil --dns | head -20        # which servers are configured
dig example.com +short         # ask via the system resolv setup
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com +short   # bypass your configured server

head: Result
Meaning
Next step
rows: check Wi-Fi, `ifconfig en0`, `route -n get default`, then the router
try another server, flush the cache
your configured DNS server is down or filtered
renew the lease, restart the router

blocks.code:
networksetup -listallnetworkservices
networksetup -getdnsservers Wi-Fi
sudo networksetup -setdnsservers Wi-Fi 1.1.1.1 9.9.9.9      # change
sudo networksetup -setdnsservers Wi-Fi Empty                # back to DHCP-provided
sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder
sudo ipconfig set en0 DHCP                                   # renew the lease

blocks.text: Wi-Fi itself: toggle it from the menu bar, forget and rejoin the network, check the signal with `system_profiler SPAirPortDataType | head -40`, and test another device to see whether the router or your Mac is at fault. A VPN or a content filter can replace your resolvers; `scutil --dns` shows who is answering.
Address already in use
Symptoms:

blocks.code:
OSError: [Errno 48] Address already in use
Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000

blocks.text: Cause: another process is already listening on that port (a ghost of your last run, or a macOS service; AirPlay Receiver occupies 5000 and 7000). Find it, then decide whether to stop it or use another port.

blocks.code: lsof -nP -iTCP:{{port}} -sTCP:LISTEN

$ lsof -nP -iTCP:8000 -sTCP:LISTEN
COMMAND   PID USER   FD   TYPE             DEVICE SIZE/OFF NODE NAME
Python  41233 you     4u  IPv6 0x7a1c2e5b3d4f9a8c      0t0  TCP *:8000 (LISTEN)

kill 41233                    # SIGTERM first
kill -9 41233                 # only if it ignores SIGTERM
python3 -m http.server 8001   # or simply choose a free port

blocks.text: If the process belongs to another user or you do not recognise it, do not kill it. For 5000 and 7000, turn off System Settings > General > AirDrop & Handoff > AirPlay Receiver, or use another port.

blocks.title: Create and clear a port conflict

task.text: Start two copies of the built-in web server on the same port and resolve the conflict.

items.text: In one Terminal tab run `python3 -m http.server 8000`.
In a second tab run the same command and read the error.
In the second tab find the process holding the port with `lsof` and stop it.

hints: Add `-sTCP:LISTEN` so `lsof` hides connections that are not the listener.
blocks.solution:
lsof -nP -iTCP:8000 -sTCP:LISTEN
kill <PID from the second column>
python3 -m http.server 8000

why.text: A port can have only one listener per address. The second program's `bind()` call fails with errno 48. `lsof` maps the port to a process, and `kill` (SIGTERM) lets it close the socket. `Ctrl+C` in the first tab does the same job.

blocks.text: curl: (60) certificate problem
Symptom:

blocks.code: curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate

blocks.text: Cause: curl could not build a trusted chain to the server's certificate. Common reasons: a wrong system clock, a TLS-inspecting proxy, a self-signed certificate on your own server, or a stale CA bundle in a Homebrew curl.

blocks.code:
date                                           # clock far off breaks validation
curl -vI https://{{domain}} 2>&1 | grep -iE 'issuer|expire|subject'
openssl s_client -connect {{domain}}:443 -servername {{domain}} </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates
curl -k https://{{host}}:8443/                 # -k skips verification: only for a server you own

blocks.text: tcpdump and nmap permission errors
Symptoms:

blocks.code:
tcpdump: en0: You don't have permission to capture on that device
You requested a scan type which requires root privileges.

blocks.text: Cause: raw packet capture and SYN or OS scans need root.

blocks.code:
sudo tcpdump -i en0 -nn -c 10
sudo nmap -sS -F {{host}}          # only hosts you own or may test
nmap -sT -F {{host}}               # a connect scan needs no root

blocks.text: `sudo` shows no characters while you type the password. That is normal, not a hang: type it and press [[Enter]].
SSH
Host key changed
Symptom:

blocks.code:
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
@    WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!     @
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
...
Offending ECDSA key in /Users/you/.ssh/known_hosts:12
Host key verification failed.

blocks.text: Cause: the key presented by that address differs from the one saved in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. Usual innocent reasons: you reinstalled the server (a Pi reflashed), the address now belongs to another machine, or the server was rebuilt. A man-in-the-middle is the unusual one; if you did not change the server, find out why before continuing.

blocks.code:
ssh-keygen -R {{host}}            # remove the stale entry (also try the IP)
ssh {{sshuser}}@{{host}}          # accept the new fingerprint after checking it
ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 {{host}}   # show the key the host offers now

blocks.text: The line number in the message (`known_hosts:12`) is the entry to delete by hand if `-R` does not match.
Permission denied (publickey)
Symptoms:

blocks.code:
{{sshuser}}@{{host}}: Permission denied (publickey).
Too many authentication failures

blocks.text: Cause: the server accepted no key you offered. Check which keys are tried, which user you are, and the server's permissions.
`Too many authentication failures` means the agent offered more keys than the server allows attempts for. Pin the right one in `~/.ssh/config`:
Unprotected private key file
Symptom:

blocks.code:
WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!
Permissions 0644 for '/Users/you/.ssh/id_ed25519' are too open.

chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

blocks.text: The agent forgets your key after every reboot
Symptom: you are asked for the key passphrase again each session.
Fix: store it in the macOS Keychain and tell SSH to use it, in `~/.ssh/config`:

blocks.code:
Host *
  AddKeysToAgent yes
  UseKeychain yes
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

blocks.text: Connection refused or timed out

head: Message
Meaning
Check
rows: `ssh: connect to host {{host}} port 22: Connection refused`
enable Remote Login on a Mac (System Settings > General > Sharing), or start `sshd` on the server
`ssh: connect to host {{host}} port 22: Operation timed out`

blocks.text: Checkpoint

questions.q: A Homebrew Python refuses `pip install` with `externally-managed-environment`. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Create and activate a venv, then install inside it

questions.why: PEP 668 protects the Python that Homebrew manages. A venv gives your project its own site-packages, so nothing global is modified.

questions.q: `zsh: no matches found: requests[security]` means which of these?

options.text: the package does not exist on PyPI
zsh tried to expand the brackets as a glob; quote the argument

questions.why: zsh globs before running the command. Quoting passes the literal string to pip.

questions.q: `ssh` prints `REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!`. Which command removes the stale entry?
questions.why: `ssh-keygen -R hostname` deletes that host's entries from `known_hosts`. Check why the key changed before reconnecting.

questions.q: Which command shows what is listening on TCP port 8000 on macOS?
questions.why: macOS has no `ss`, and its `netstat -p` takes a protocol, not a port. `lsof` maps listening sockets to processes.

questions.q: Running a script prints `bad interpreter: /bin/bash^M: no such file or directory`. What is wrong?

options.text: The file uses CRLF line endings
The shebang points to a directory
The script has no trailing newline

questions.why: The carriage return becomes part of the interpreter name. Remove it with `tr -d '\r'` or `sed -i '' $'s/\r$//'`.

blocks.text: Next: back to the [cheat sheets](#cheats), or into [Troubleshooting](#troubleshoot) for the network method.

terms.def: the Python standard that lets a distribution mark an interpreter as externally managed so pip will not modify it
Transparency, Consent and Control, the macOS system that gates app access to private folders and devices
System Integrity Protection, which keeps system folders read-only even for root
the macOS check that verifies downloaded apps before first launch
the extended attribute `com.apple.quarantine` set on downloaded files
the two-byte Windows line ending, carriage return plus line feed
the file where SSH records each server's public key
